title: Free-body diagrams: cutting an object free to see every force on it
examples: How do I draw a free-body diagram?
What forces act on a car parked on a slope?
Why is the normal force not equal to the weight on a ramp?

forces.ask: Why is the normal force perpendicular to the surface?

explain.say: Picture a car parked on a steep street in Shimla or San Francisco. It does not move, so every force on it must cancel. A free-body diagram is a sketch where you cut the car free from the world and draw only the forces acting on it, as arrows. Let us build one together.

draw.text: Car: 1200 kg, parked on a 20 degree slope

explain.say: First, the weight. It always points straight down, towards the centre of the Earth. For a 1200 kilogram car it is 1200 times 9.81, about 11.8 kilonewtons. See the long arrow pointing down? Which way would the car go if weight were the only force?

forces.label: Weight 11.8 kN
forces.ask: Why does weight always point straight down?

forces.label: Normal 11.1 kN
forces.ask: Why is the normal force perpendicular to the surface?

explain.say: Downhill, of course! Now the road pushes back. That push, the normal force, is always at right angles to the surface, so on a 20 degree slope it tilts too. It only has to balance the part of the weight pressing into the road: 11.8 times cos 20, about 11.1 kilonewtons. Is it bigger or smaller than the weight?

forces.label: Weight 11.8 kN
forces.ask: Why does weight always point straight down?

forces.label: Normal 11.1 kN
forces.ask: Why is the normal force perpendicular to the surface?

draw.text: N = W cos θ = 11.8 × cos 20° = 11.1 kN

explain.say: Smaller, yes. The last arrow is friction, acting up the slope along the road. It stops the car sliding by balancing the downhill part of the weight: 11.8 times sin 20, about 4.0 kilonewtons. Look at the short arrow pointing up the hill. What would happen on ice, with almost no friction?

draw.text: F = W sin θ = 11.8 × sin 20° = 4.0 kN

explain.say: It would slide away! Brilliant work. Exam tip: on any slope, tilt your x and y axes to lie along and across the surface. Then only the weight needs splitting into parts. Challenge: how does each force change if the slope gets steeper?

faq.a: It is a sketch of one object cut free from its surroundings, with every external force drawn as an arrow at the point where it acts. It is the first step in almost every mechanics problem.

faq.q: Why does weight always point straight down?
faq.a: Weight is the pull of gravity, which acts towards the centre of the Earth, so it is vertical whatever the slope. Its size is mass times g, 9.81 metres per second squared.
asks: direction of weight on a slope

faq.q: Why is the normal force perpendicular to the surface?
faq.a: A surface can only push straight out of itself. Any force along the surface is called friction and is drawn separately. On a slope the normal force equals the weight times the cosine of the angle.
asks: why is normal force less than weight on a ramp

faq.a: Friction always opposes the sliding, or the tendency to slide. A car parked on a hill tends to roll downhill, so friction acts up the slope.
asks: direction of friction on an incline

faq.q: What should I leave out of a free-body diagram?
faq.a: Leave out the forces the object exerts on other things, and internal forces between its own parts. Only forces from outside acting on the object belong on the diagram.

facts: On a slope of angle theta, the normal force on a resting object is its weight times cos theta.
The force of gravity on a 1 kg mass near the Earth's surface is about 9.81 newtons.

quiz.say: A 50 kilogram crate rests on a 30 degree ramp. What friction force holds it still? Use g equals 9.81.
quiz.show: A 50 kg crate rests on a 30° ramp. Friction holding it? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
quiz.why: Friction balances the downhill part of the weight: 50 × 9.81 × sin 30° = 245 N.

wrong.1: That uses cos 30°, which gives the normal force, not friction.
wrong.2: That is the full weight; only part of it acts along the slope.

quiz.say: Which force should NOT appear on the free-body diagram of a book resting on a table?
quiz.show: Which force does NOT belong on the FBD of a book on a table?

options.show: The table pushing up on the book

quiz.why: That force acts on the table, not on the book, so it belongs on the table's diagram.

wrong.0: Gravity acts on the book, so its weight belongs on the diagram.
wrong.1: The table's push acts on the book, so it belongs on the diagram.
